title: Access Token Manipulation: Make and Impersonate Token
shortTitle: Access Token Manipulation: Make and Impersonate Token
summary: Making and impersonating a token covers the case where the attacker builds a brand new access token instead of copying one that already exists in memory. With a valid username and password, a credential-carrying logon interface such as LogonUser creates a fresh logon session for that account and hands back the access token for it, which the attacker can then assign to a thread and use for the rest of the operation. The critical difference from token theft is the prerequisite: theft needs a live session already present on the host and administrator rights to reach it, while this path needs the account secret and works even when the target user is nowhere near the machine and has never logged on to it. Because a genuine authentication happens first, the telemetry shows a real logon session, often of the interactive or new-credentials type, from an account that has no business on that host, followed by process and file activity attributed to it. Defenders treat a credential logon on a workstation for an account that never works there, particularly outside business hours or from a service account, as the strongest single indicator, and pair it with the absence of the usual remote access pattern that would justify that session.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker uses a username and password they already stole to create a fresh digital pass. The pass belongs to that real user account, and the attacker then gives it to a program. Nothing is copied from another running program, so the pass is brand new.
beginner.whyItMatters: Stolen credentials are common, and this method turns them into immediate power on the machine. It works even when the real user is at home and not logged in. The activity includes a genuine logon, so it blends into normal authentication traffic. Noticing it depends on knowing which accounts should ever log on to which machines.
howItWorks: The attacker already holds a valid username and password for the victim account.
An attacker uses a built in Windows interface to open a new logon session with those credentials.
The function returns a new pass, called an access token, that belongs to that account.
The attacker assigns the new pass to a thread, meaning one worker inside their program.
That worker then opens files or services as the real user, without stealing anything.
A real logon event is recorded, so the authentication itself looks valid in the logs.
beginner.example: Picture a shared flat where each person has their own door key. A guest finds a housemate spare key hanging in the kitchen and copies the cut. The guest does not take the original and does not need the housemate to be home. The front door opens like a normal arrival, and the entrance camera simply shows the key being used, not who used it.
takeaways: This creates a new pass from credentials, so no live session needs to exist on the host.
A genuine logon event is logged, which makes the authentication look normal on its own.
Alert on accounts logging on to machines where they have no legitimate reason to be.

objectives: Explain how a new access token is produced from a username and password.
State clearly how this sub-technique differs from stealing an existing token.
Describe why a legitimate logon session appears in the logs during this behaviour.
Identify the logon event types that matter when reviewing credential based token use.
Explain why knowing normal account to host relationships is essential for detection.
